content:
Earlier this year, I replaced a gas-powered lawn mower with a robotic mower that can be controlled via iPhone. Users can manually drive the robot along the lawn's perimeter to create a virtual map. Once set up, the robot will automatically mow according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I've been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation approach, and after several weeks of testing, I think for many people this one may be easier to use.

Camera-assisted automatic map creation

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each robot understands your lawn.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the perimeter with my iPhone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 instead uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. Three cameras allow the mower to automatically map out the lawn without burying boundary wires or installing a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process takes longer, but I think it may be simpler for people who are less tech-savvy.

To verify this claim, I had my mother, who lives in another state, install and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She reported that everything worked fine. However, I'm not entirely sure she had the patience to first manually drive the robot around the entire perimeter with her phone and then mark out all the areas to avoid.

The automatic mapping caused a minor issue in my front yard. There's no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's, so the TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn in my map.

I marked that area as a no-go zone in the app, and the problem was resolved. That said, if there's no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, you need to pay extra attention during the initial map creation.

Peeking through the mower's camera

The camera on the TerraMow also brings one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used iPhone screen mirroring on my Mac to keep this view open in a large window. I could sit inside working while watching from the mower's perspective as it navigated the backyard.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun and sometimes helps explain why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 doesn't offer a similar camera view feature.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps have quite a bit in common. Both support scheduled tasks, mowing mode adjustments, zone划分, no-go zone marking, and remote control of the mower.

The TerraMow has a particularly nice variation on that last feature. In addition to the traditional left-right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-hand joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and use your thumb to steer the mower.

Manually driving the mower with the iPhone isn't the primary use of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically on a preset schedule without any intervention. That said, the TerraMow's joystick mode is fun for cleaning up small patches the robot missed.

Sometimes, I almost felt like I was controlling the robot by telekinesis (that fun kind of telekinesis). I'd walk alongside the mower holding my iPhone, barely moving my thumb, and the robot would already follow my directions.

Every robotic mower app should copy this control design.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was louder while running.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow "noisy," but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot runs very quietly—quiet enough that it's easy to forget it's still running, including when it mows at night using its headlight.

Since the TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. Therefore, scheduling daytime mowing becomes more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that covers the charging dock, while the Anthbot's garage must be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow performed reliably. I relied on it for daily mowing for several consecutive weeks without needing to intervene.

When adaptive mapping gets too clever

The visual intelligence that makes the TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts the map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes some time, during which you can't perform other operations in the app.

After several consecutive days of rain, I encountered an interesting edge case. There was a puddle in one spot in the yard, and the TerraMow reasonably avoided that area on its next run.

Within the skipped circular area, the weeds grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to interpret the growth there as an object to continue avoiding, and even after the ground dried out, the area was still being ignored.

I used the remote control function in the app to manually drive the mower there to cut the taller grass, and the problem was resolved. Once the area returned to its normal appearance, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regular edging can also help the TerraMow reach its boundaries more confidently. Tall grass growing along fuzzy boundary lines might otherwise be mistaken for obstacles rather than part of the mowing area.

The Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. This method requires more upfront work, but it also avoids the map "changing its mind" about the same patch of grass.

9to5Mac Conclusion

After using both systems, for most people I lean toward recommending the TerraMow's camera approach.

For me, burying boundary wires is completely impractical, and installing an RTK base station means having to place, power, and maintain additional hardware. The TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. Initial map creation takes longer, invisible property boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook overgrown grass as a permanent obstacle.

These issues are still manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, engaging real-time camera footage, and the best manual control experience of any robotic mower app I've used.

I do enjoy working on the yard, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this task over to a robot frees up my time for landscaping, edging, and detail work while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 excels in this regard, and I'd recommend it, especially for anyone who wants a robotic mower but doesn't want to bury boundary wires, install an RTK antenna, or walk the entire yard with their phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at $999 after applying a $200 coupon on the site. It's also available for purchase on TerraMow's official website.
